topic: What if you opened a McDonald's in ancient Rome?

script.text: Here's how it starts. You and your little sister Ellie are walking home with a bag of takeaway. A flash. A ringing in your ears.
And then you're standing in a narrow street that smells like smoke, donkeys and fish sauce. Everyone is wearing sheets. Okay, tunics. A man with a cart shouts at you in Latin.
A coin in the dirt has an emperor's face on it. Nero. It's the summer of the year sixty-four, and this is Rome. The biggest city in the world, with around a million people.

So here are the rules. There's no way back. You have the clothes you're wearing, a phone with no signal, and one cold burger in a paper bag. That's it. No fridge. No fryer. No electricity. Not one machine.
But you have something nobody else in Rome has. You know exactly how a fast food restaurant works. The same food, every time, ready in one minute.
And one more thing. Rome, in the summer of sixty-four. It sounds familiar. Something from history class. You just can't remember what.

science.claim: Rome had around a million people in the first century AD, the largest city in the world.
science.working: Modern estimates for Rome under the early emperors range from about 800,000 to over a million; 'around a million' is the usual figure.
science.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Rome: The imperial city'; W. Scheidel, 'Roman population size' (2008)
